requirementRaw: Add JWT-based bearer token authentication to the URL shortener's management endpoints (create, retrieve metadata, and delete). The public redirect endpoint should remain unauthenticated. Include a way to issue a token, and validate the token on protected endpoints using Spring Security.

output.normalized_spec: Integrate Spring Security into the existing URL shortener service to enforce JWT bearer token authentication on management endpoints (create short URL, retrieve metadata, delete short URL), while leaving the public redirect endpoint unauthenticated and accessible to all clients. Provide a token issuance endpoint that authenticates a client/user and returns a signed JWT, and implement a security filter chain that validates the JWT's signature, expiration, and claims on each request to protected endpoints, rejecting invalid or missing tokens with 401 Unauthorized. Non-functional requirements include use of a standard signing algorithm (e.g., HS256 or RS256), configurable token expiration, and no disruption to existing unauthenticated redirect functionality.
assumptions: There is an existing user/client identity store or a simple credential set (e.g., username/password or API key) used to issue tokens; if not, a minimal in-memory or config-based credential store will be introduced.
JWT will be signed using a symmetric secret (HS256) unless asymmetric signing is explicitly required, with the secret stored in application configuration/environment variables.
Token issuance endpoint (e.g., /auth/token or /login) is itself unauthenticated or uses basic credential validation, and is out of scope for JWT protection.
No refresh token or logout/revocation mechanism is required unless specified.
Existing management endpoints' request/response contracts remain unchanged except for the addition of the Authorization header requirement.
open_ambiguities: What identity/credential source should be used to authenticate users when issuing a token (existing user DB, hardcoded service account, API key, third-party IdP)?
Should tokens include role/scope claims for differentiated access control, or is authentication alone (no authorization levels) sufficient?
What is the desired token expiration duration, and is token refresh or revocation needed?
Should the signing key be symmetric (HS256) or asymmetric (RS256), and how should it be managed/rotated?

output.api_contract: Add POST /auth/token (unauthenticated) accepting username/password (or API key) credentials, returning a signed JWT with expiration in the response body. Existing endpoints POST /urls (create), GET /urls/{code} (metadata), and DELETE /urls/{code} (delete) in shortener-service/controller now require a valid 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' header, returning 401 Unauthorized if missing/invalid/expired. GET /{code} redirect endpoint remains fully unauthenticated with no contract changes. Request/response bodies of management endpoints are otherwise unchanged.
output.data_model: Introduce a lightweight Credential/User entity (username, hashed password or API key, optional roles field for future use) backing a minimal in-memory or config-based credential store, since no existing identity store was confirmed. Existing shortener-service/model entities (ShortUrl: code, originalUrl, createdAt, metadata) remain unchanged. JWT claims include subject (username), issuedAt, expiration, and signature; no new persistent entity is required for tokens since revocation/refresh is out of scope.
output.short_code_strategy: No change to existing short code generation logic in shortener-service; this design only adds authentication around existing create/retrieve/delete operations and does not alter how codes are generated.
output.caching_strategy: Deferred — the public redirect endpoint remains unauthenticated and untouched, so any existing or future redirect caching is unaffected by this change; no new caching is introduced for JWT validation, though stateless JWT verification (signature/expiration check per request) inherently avoids server-side session storage.
